subject: Everyday Science
q: The Earth’s axis is tilted at an angle of about ______ from the perpendicular to its orbit.
explanation: The axis is tilted by about 23.5°, which fixes the positions of the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn at 23.5° north and south.

subject: Everyday Science
q: In the Northern Hemisphere, the longest day of the year (summer solstice) falls on about:
explanation: Around 21 June the North Pole is tilted most towards the Sun, which is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer.

subject: Everyday Science
q: On the days of the equinoxes (around 21 March and 23 September), the midday Sun is directly overhead at the:
explanation: At the equinoxes neither hemisphere tilts towards the Sun, so the Sun is overhead at the equator and day and night are nearly equal everywhere.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The world is divided into how many time zones?
explanation: The Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, so dividing it into 15° slices gives 24 standard time zones, each about one hour apart.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The International Date Line roughly follows the:
explanation: The Date Line lies mostly along the 180° meridian in the Pacific; crossing it changes the calendar date by one day.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A leap year with an extra day is added every four years because:
o: The Moon’s orbit changes every four years
The Earth slows down every four years
The Earth takes about 365¼ days to orbit the Sun
explanation: The four extra quarter-days add up to one full day, which is added as 29 February to keep the calendar in step with the seasons.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The innermost layer of the Earth is the:
explanation: The Earth has three main layers: the thin outer crust, the thick mantle and the central core.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The Earth’s core is composed mainly of:
explanation: Seismic studies and the Earth’s density show that the core is mostly iron with some nickel: a liquid outer core around a solid inner core.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The Earth’s magnetic field is believed to be produced by:
o: Movement of molten iron in the outer core
explanation: Convection currents of liquid iron in the outer core, combined with the Earth’s rotation, generate electric currents that create the magnetic field.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The Earth’s rigid outer shell (lithosphere) is broken into large moving pieces called:
explanation: The lithosphere consists of several major and many minor plates that move slowly over the softer mantle beneath.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A plate boundary where two plates slide horizontally past each other is called a:
explanation: At transform boundaries, such as the San Andreas Fault, plates grind past one another, causing frequent earthquakes but little volcanic activity.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The Himalayas were formed by the collision of the Indian plate with the:
explanation: As the Indian plate pushed northward into Eurasia, the crust between them was folded and uplifted into the Himalayas, which are still rising.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The theory of continental drift was proposed by:
explanation: In 1912 Wegener suggested that the continents were once joined in a supercontinent, Pangaea, and have slowly drifted apart.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which seismic waves cannot travel through liquids?
explanation: S-waves are shear waves and liquids cannot resist shearing; their absence on the far side of the Earth showed that the outer core is liquid.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Molten rock that pours out onto the Earth’s surface during a volcanic eruption is called:
explanation: Molten rock below ground is called magma; once it erupts onto the surface it is called lava.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The “Ring of Fire”, famous for frequent earthquakes and volcanic eruptions, surrounds the:
explanation: Plate boundaries around the Pacific Ocean host about three-quarters of the world’s active volcanoes and most large earthquakes.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Pumice, a volcanic rock, can float on water because it:
o: Is full of tiny gas holes
explanation: Pumice forms when gas-rich lava cools very quickly, trapping countless bubbles that make the rock lighter than water.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Rocks formed by the cooling and solidification of magma or lava are called:
explanation: Igneous rocks such as granite and basalt form from molten material; the word comes from the Latin for fire.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Marble is a metamorphic rock formed from:
explanation: Heat and pressure recrystallise limestone into marble, which is why both are made of calcium carbonate.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Fossils are most commonly found in:
explanation: Sedimentary rocks form from layers of sediment that can bury and preserve remains of organisms; heat destroys fossils in the other rock types.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The aurora (northern and southern lights) is caused by:
o: Charged particles from the Sun striking gases in the upper atmosphere
Reflection of sunlight from polar ice
explanation: The solar wind’s charged particles are guided by the Earth’s magnetic field towards the poles, where they make atmospheric gases glow.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The part of the CPU that performs arithmetic and logical operations is the:
explanation: The ALU carries out calculations and comparisons, while the control unit directs the flow of instructions and data.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The main circuit board of a computer, to which the CPU, memory and other components are connected, is the:
explanation: The motherboard holds the processor and memory and provides the connections through which all components communicate.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which component connects a computer to external peripherals such as printers and keyboards?
explanation: Input/output ports such as USB and HDMI provide the physical connection points for external devices.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Give the name of the USB port which exists in all modern computers:
explanation: USB stands for Universal Serial Bus, a standard for connecting and powering peripherals through one type of port.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which of the following works as both an input and an output device?
explanation: A touchscreen displays output and also accepts input from the user’s touch.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Drum printers belong to which of the following category?
explanation: A drum printer prints a whole line at a time using a rotating drum of characters, so it is classed as a line printer.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which of the following is an impact printer?
explanation: A dot-matrix printer forms characters by striking pins against an inked ribbon, so the print head physically hits the paper.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The resolution of a printer is usually expressed in:
explanation: More dots per inch means finer detail; pages per minute measures speed instead.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Technology that converts printed or scanned text into editable computer text is called:
explanation: OCR software recognises the shapes of letters in an image and turns them into text characters that can be edited and searched.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Banks use MICR technology mainly to read:
o: Numbers printed in magnetic ink on cheques
explanation: Magnetic Ink Character Recognition reads the special characters at the bottom of cheques quickly and reliably, even if they are overwritten.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Computers store and process all data internally in the form of:
explanation: Electronic circuits have two stable states (on and off), which are represented by the binary digits 1 and 0.

subject: Everyday Science
q: One byte is equal to:
explanation: A byte is a group of eight bits and can represent 256 different values, enough for one character of text.

subject: Everyday Science
q: RAM is called volatile memory because:
o: It can only be read, not written
It is stored on a spinning disk
It is slower than a hard disk
Its contents are lost when the power is switched off
explanation: RAM holds programs and data only while the computer is powered; anything not saved to storage disappears when it is turned off.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which of the following is a non-volatile memory?
explanation: ROM keeps its contents without power, which is why it is used to hold start-up firmware.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The small, very fast memory between the CPU and main memory that holds frequently used data is called:
explanation: Cache stores copies of data the processor is likely to need next, so it does not have to wait for slower RAM.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The BIOS, which checks the hardware and starts the computer when it is switched on, is stored in:
explanation: Start-up instructions must survive power-off, so the BIOS is kept in a non-volatile ROM or flash firmware chip on the motherboard.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Virtual memory is:
o: Part of the hard disk used as an extension of RAM
explanation: When RAM is full, the operating system moves less-used data to a reserved area of the disk, making the computer appear to have more memory.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A solid-state drive (SSD) differs from a traditional hard disk mainly because it:
o: Stores data on spinning magnetic platters
Loses its data when the power is off
Can only be read, not written
Uses flash memory and has no moving parts
explanation: SSDs store data on flash memory chips, making them faster, quieter and more shock-resistant than hard disks with rotating platters.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Data on a CD or DVD is read using:
explanation: Optical discs store data as tiny pits on a reflective surface, which a laser reads by detecting changes in reflected light.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which of the following is an operating system?
explanation: Linux manages hardware and runs other programs, which is the job of an operating system; the others are application programs.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A program that translates an entire high-level language program into machine code before it is run is called a:
explanation: A compiler translates the whole source program at once, whereas an interpreter translates and executes it line by line.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A program written in assembly language is converted into machine code by an:
explanation: An assembler translates the mnemonic instructions of assembly language into the binary instructions the processor executes.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Software whose source code is freely available for anyone to study, modify and share is called:
explanation: Open-source licences allow anyone to view and improve the code; Linux and Firefox are well-known examples.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A programming language that can be run on different types of computers with little or no change is a:
explanation: High-level languages are machine-independent; translators convert them for each processor, whereas machine and assembly code are tied to one processor type.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem is called an:
explanation: An algorithm is a finite, ordered sequence of steps; computer programs are algorithms written in a programming language.

subject: Everyday Science
q: GUI, the type of interface that uses windows, icons and menus, stands for:
explanation: A graphical user interface lets users operate a computer by pointing and clicking on visual elements instead of typing commands.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The process of starting a computer and loading its operating system into memory is called:
explanation: When powered on, firmware tests the hardware and loads the operating system; this start-up sequence is booting.

subject: Everyday Science
q: When text is cut or copied, it is held temporarily in the:
explanation: The clipboard is a temporary storage area in memory from which copied or cut data can be pasted elsewhere.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The smallest single element of a digital image on a screen is called a:
explanation: A digital image is a grid of picture elements (pixels), each showing one colour; more pixels mean higher resolution.

subject: Everyday Science
q: ASCII is a:
o: Code for representing text characters as numbers
explanation: The American Standard Code for Information Interchange assigns a number to each letter, digit and symbol so that computers can store text.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The hexadecimal number system uses base:
explanation: Hexadecimal uses sixteen symbols, 0–9 and A–F, and is a compact way of writing binary values.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A network of computers within a single building or campus is called a:
explanation: A Local Area Network connects devices over a small area such as an office, school or home.

subject: Everyday Science
q: In which network topology are all computers connected to a central hub or switch?
explanation: In a star topology each device has its own cable to a central device, so one cable failure affects only that computer.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The device that connects different networks, such as a home network and the internet, and directs data between them is a:
explanation: A router reads the destination address of each packet of data and forwards it along the best path to another network.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A modem is used to:
o: Convert digital signals to analogue signals and back for transmission
explanation: The name comes from modulator–demodulator: it converts a computer’s digital data into signals suited to telephone or cable lines and back again.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The permanent hardware address built into a device’s network adapter is called its:
explanation: The Media Access Control address is assigned by the manufacturer and identifies the network interface on a local network; an IP address is assigned for routing.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The protocol which assigns IP addresses to clients connected to the internet is:
explanation: DHCP automatically gives each device joining a network an IP address and other settings, so they need not be configured by hand.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The Domain Name System (DNS) on the internet is used to:
o: Translate website names into IP addresses
explanation: DNS works like a phone book, converting names such as example.com into the numeric addresses computers use.

subject: Everyday Science
q: HTTP, used for web pages, stands for:
explanation: HTTP is the protocol by which web browsers request pages from web servers and receive them.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The “S” in HTTPS indicates that the connection is:
explanation: HTTPS encrypts data between the browser and the website, protecting passwords and payment details from being read in transit.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which protocol is used to send email from one mail server to another?
explanation: The Simple Mail Transfer Protocol handles the sending and relaying of email between servers.

subject: Everyday Science
q: FTP is a standard protocol used for:
o: Sending text messages on mobile phones
Transferring files between computers over a network
explanation: The File Transfer Protocol is designed for uploading and downloading files between a client and a server.

subject: Everyday Science
q: IPv6 was introduced mainly because:
o: IPv4 did not work with wireless networks
The supply of IPv4 addresses was running out
IPv4 was too expensive to use
explanation: IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses (about 4.3 billion); IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, providing a practically unlimited number.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The address of a web page, such as https://www.example.com, is called a:
explanation: URL stands for Uniform Resource Locator, the unique address that tells a browser where to find a resource on the web.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The World Wide Web was invented by:
explanation: Tim Berners-Lee proposed the web at CERN in 1989, creating HTTP, HTML and the first web browser.

subject: Everyday Science
q: HTML is mainly used to:
explanation: HyperText Markup Language uses tags to define headings, paragraphs, links and images on web pages.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which statement correctly describes the World Wide Web?
o: It is another name for the internet itself
It is a type of network cable
It is a system used only for sending email
It is a system of linked web pages accessed over the internet
explanation: The internet is the global network of connected computers; the web is one service that runs on it, alongside email and file transfer.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Bluetooth is a technology used for:
explanation: Bluetooth links nearby devices such as phones, earphones and keyboards by low-power radio over distances of roughly 10 metres.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Wi-Fi networks are based on which family of IEEE standards?
explanation: Wireless LANs follow the IEEE 802.11 family of standards; 802.3 is wired Ethernet.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Ethernet is the most common technology for:
explanation: Ethernet defines how devices on a wired LAN exchange data through cables and switches.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The data transfer speed (bandwidth) of an internet connection is usually measured in:
explanation: Connection speeds are expressed in bits per second, commonly megabits per second (Mbps).

subject: Everyday Science
q: The network that is regarded as the forerunner of today’s internet was:
explanation: ARPANET, funded by the US Department of Defense and first operating in 1969, pioneered packet switching and the protocols that became the internet.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Software designed to damage a computer or steal information is generally called:
explanation: Malware (malicious software) covers viruses, worms, trojans, spyware and ransomware.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A malicious program that copies itself and spreads across networks on its own, without attaching to other files, is a:
explanation: Unlike a virus, which needs a host file and user action, a worm spreads by itself from computer to computer through network weaknesses.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A Trojan horse is malware that:
o: Disguises itself as useful or legitimate software
explanation: Like the wooden horse of legend, it tricks users into installing it and then performs harmful actions secretly.
